disclaimer: Education, not financial or legal advice. Facts as at October 2026.

scenes.headline: 10 corporate disasters that could have been prevented
scenes.body: Enron. Lehman. FTX. Volkswagen. Boeing. And five more.
scenes.voiceover: What if I told you that some of the biggest corporate disasters in history didn't happen because nobody saw the warning signs? They happened because someone saw them, and the system failed to respond.

scenes.headline: Someone always saw it coming.
scenes.voiceover: Employees raised concerns. Auditors found problems. Journalists investigated. Regulators received warnings. And yet, in case after case, the problems continued until the truth could no longer be hidden.

scenes.headline: What happened, how it was exposed, and where they are now.
scenes.voiceover: From Enron to Lehman Brothers, Volkswagen, F T X and Boeing, these aren't simply stories about companies that failed. They are stories about governance failures. For each one, we're asking: what happened? What was the biggest trigger? How was it finally exposed? Who was held responsible? And where are they now?

scenes.headline: Enron
scenes.voiceover: Number one. Enron. Two thousand and one.

scenes.name: Enron
scenes.headline: Debt and losses hidden off the balance sheet
scenes.voiceover: Before the scandal, Enron looked like the future. It was one of America's most admired companies. But underneath the success, Enron was carrying enormous amounts of debt and losses that investors weren't seeing. It used complicated special-purpose entities to keep liabilities away from its main balance sheet. On paper, Enron looked profitable. Behind the scenes, it was becoming increasingly unstable.
scenes.body: Complex special-purpose entities kept liabilities out of sight.

scenes.name: Enron
scenes.headline: The CEO quit. Then an executive spoke up.
scenes.voiceover: C E O Jeffrey Skilling suddenly resigned in August two thousand and one. Shortly afterwards, Enron executive Sherron Watkins warned chairman Kenneth Lay that the company's accounting could cause it to collapse.
scenes.body: Sherron Watkins warned chairman Kenneth Lay the accounting could sink the company.

scenes.name: Enron
scenes.headline: Bankrupt by December 2001
scenes.voiceover: The share price collapsed, and in December two thousand and one, Enron filed for bankruptcy. More than seventy-four billion dollars in shareholder value disappeared.

scenes.name: Enron
scenes.headline: Prison for the CFO and CEO. The auditor fell too.
scenes.voiceover: C F O Andrew Fastow pleaded guilty and received a prison sentence. Jeffrey Skilling was convicted and eventually sentenced to fourteen years in prison, after his original sentence was reduced. Kenneth Lay was convicted but died before sentencing. And auditor Arthur Andersen was convicted of obstruction of justice, and effectively collapsed as a major auditing business.

scenes.name: Enron
scenes.headline: Enron and Arthur Andersen are both gone
scenes.voiceover: How was it caught? Falling share prices, internal warnings, investigative scrutiny and increasingly impossible accounting. Today, Enron is gone. Arthur Andersen's former audit business is gone. Skilling eventually returned to business after prison.

scenes.name: Enron
scenes.headline: A warning that isn't acted on isn't a control.
scenes.voiceover: The lesson: a warning that isn't acted upon isn't really a control.

scenes.headline: WorldCom
scenes.voiceover: Number two. WorldCom. Two thousand and two.

scenes.name: WorldCom
scenes.headline: Everyday costs booked as investments
scenes.voiceover: WorldCom was one of America's largest telecommunications companies, but its profits were falling. Instead of accepting lower profits, management changed the accounting. Ordinary operating expenses were recorded as capital investments. Eventually, the improper accounting amounted to almost eleven billion dollars.

scenes.name: WorldCom
scenes.headline: Internal audit followed the entries
scenes.voiceover: The breakthrough came from an internal audit team led by Cynthia Cooper. Her team refused to accept management's explanations, investigated suspicious entries, and followed them to their source, uncovering the scale of the manipulation.
scenes.body: Cynthia Cooper's team refused to accept management's explanations.

scenes.name: WorldCom
scenes.headline: 25 years for the CEO
scenes.voiceover: WorldCom filed for bankruptcy. C E O Bernard Ebbers was convicted and sentenced to twenty-five years in prison. C F O Scott Sullivan pleaded guilty and cooperated.

stat.label: Prison sentence for CEO Bernard Ebbers

scenes.name: WorldCom
scenes.headline: Absorbed into MCI, then Verizon
scenes.voiceover: WorldCom eventually emerged as M C I, before later becoming part of Verizon. It no longer exists independently. Bernard Ebbers died in twenty twenty.

scenes.name: WorldCom
scenes.headline: Reward numbers over truth, and the numbers stop meaning anything.
scenes.voiceover: The lesson: if employees are rewarded for producing numbers rather than producing the truth, the numbers eventually become meaningless.

scenes.headline: Lehman Brothers
scenes.voiceover: Number three. Lehman Brothers. Two thousand and eight.

scenes.name: Lehman Brothers
scenes.headline: A financial machine built on borrowed money
scenes.voiceover: Lehman Brothers had built an enormous financial machine on borrowed money. Leverage reached roughly thirty to one, while the firm was heavily exposed to the collapsing American housing market.

scenes.name: Lehman Brothers
scenes.headline: Repo 105 made leverage look smaller
scenes.voiceover: Mortgage-related assets were losing value, but Lehman still needed its financial statements to look strong. One controversial mechanism became known as Repo one-oh-five. It temporarily moved assets off the balance sheet around reporting periods, and reduced the appearance of leverage.
scenes.body: Assets moved off the balance sheet around reporting dates.

scenes.name: Lehman Brothers
scenes.headline: The largest bankruptcy in US history at the time
scenes.voiceover: Then the housing crisis accelerated. Investors lost confidence. Lehman's liquidity disappeared. On the fifteenth of September two thousand and eight, Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, at the time the largest bankruptcy in U S history.

scenes.name: Lehman Brothers
scenes.headline: Heavy criticism, but no prison
scenes.voiceover: C E O Richard Fuld faced enormous criticism, but was not criminally convicted or sent to prison. The consequences were primarily financial, regulatory and civil. It was caught when the housing collapse exposed the underlying weakness, once investors stopped trusting the balance sheet.

scenes.name: Lehman Brothers
scenes.headline: The bank is gone. The estate is still paying creditors.
scenes.voiceover: Lehman Brothers as an operating investment bank is gone, while the Lehman estate has spent years recovering assets and distributing money to creditors.

scenes.name: Lehman Brothers
scenes.headline: You don't need obvious fraud to be dangerously governed.
scenes.voiceover: The lesson: a company doesn't have to commit obvious fraud to become dangerously governed.

scenes.headline: FTX
scenes.voiceover: Number four. F T X. Twenty twenty-two.

scenes.name: FTX
scenes.headline: No independent board. Customer funds moved.
scenes.voiceover: F T X went from one of the world's biggest crypto exchanges to bankruptcy in days. Founder Sam Bankman-Fried had become a billionaire celebrity, but governance was extraordinarily weak. There was no effective independent board structure, internal controls were inadequate, and customer funds were transferred to Alameda Research, a closely connected trading firm.
scenes.body: Customer money flowed to Alameda Research, a closely connected trading firm.

scenes.name: FTX
scenes.headline: Customers wanted their money back
scenes.voiceover: Questions about Alameda's financial position, and its dependence on F T X's own token, triggered a loss of confidence. Customers withdrew money. F T X couldn't meet the withdrawals. The estimated customer shortfall was around eight billion dollars.

scenes.name: FTX
scenes.headline: 25 years. Appeal rejected in 2026.
scenes.voiceover: Bankman-Fried was convicted of fraud and conspiracy, and sentenced to twenty-five years in prison. His appeal failed in twenty twenty-six. Other executives also pleaded guilty or cooperated.

scenes.name: FTX
scenes.headline: A bankruptcy and recovery operation
scenes.voiceover: How was it caught? Investigative reporting, financial analysis, and a sudden liquidity crisis. Today, F T X is a bankruptcy and recovery operation, rather than the crypto empire it once was.

scenes.name: FTX
scenes.headline: Technology doesn't create governance.
scenes.voiceover: The lesson: technology doesn't create governance. If nobody independently controls the money, the system can still collapse.

scenes.headline: Volkswagen Dieselgate
scenes.voiceover: Number five. Volkswagen. Dieselgate. Twenty fifteen.

scenes.name: Volkswagen
scenes.headline: Software that cheated the emissions test
scenes.voiceover: Volkswagen installed software known as a defeat device in diesel vehicles. During laboratory testing, the software could recognise testing conditions and change engine behaviour. During normal driving, emissions could be dramatically higher.
scenes.body: The car behaved one way in the lab and another on the road.

scenes.name: Volkswagen
scenes.headline: Researchers tested cars on real roads
scenes.voiceover: Around eleven million vehicles were eventually affected worldwide. Researchers compared laboratory emissions with real-world driving, regulators asked questions, and the scandal exploded in twenty fifteen.

scenes.name: Volkswagen
scenes.headline: Billions in penalties and buybacks
scenes.voiceover: Billions were spent on penalties, settlements, vehicle buybacks and remediation. Executives and engineers faced criminal investigations, and former C E O Martin Winterkorn faced prosecution in Germany. Several former Volkswagen employees were convicted in the major German trial in twenty twenty-five.

scenes.name: Volkswagen
scenes.headline: VW survived, and sped up its shift to electric
scenes.voiceover: Volkswagen survived, but the scandal damaged its reputation and accelerated its shift toward electric vehicles.

scenes.name: Volkswagen
scenes.headline: When targets beat compliance, cheating looks like a solution.
scenes.voiceover: The lesson: a culture that rewards targets above compliance can make illegal behaviour look like a solution.

scenes.headline: Wells Fargo
scenes.voiceover: Number six. Wells Fargo. Twenty sixteen.

scenes.name: Wells Fargo
scenes.headline: Sales targets created millions of fake accounts
scenes.voiceover: Wells Fargo employees were under enormous pressure to meet aggressive sales targets. The result was millions of unauthorised accounts.

scenes.name: Wells Fargo
scenes.headline: Complaints, whistleblowers, regulators
scenes.voiceover: Customer complaints, employee concerns, whistleblowers and regulatory investigations eventually brought the scandal into the open. In twenty sixteen, the bank was fined, and C E O John Stumpf resigned. Former Community Bank executive Carrie Tolstedt eventually pleaded guilty to obstructing a regulatory examination.

scenes.name: Wells Fargo
scenes.headline: A cap on how big the bank could grow
scenes.voiceover: In twenty eighteen, the Federal Reserve imposed an extraordinary asset cap on the bank. In March twenty twenty-six, the Federal Reserve terminated that enforcement action, after nearly a decade of remediation.

scenes.name: Wells Fargo
scenes.headline: Still a major US bank, after a decade of repairs
scenes.voiceover: Wells Fargo survived, and remains a major U S bank, after years of governance and risk-control remediation.

scenes.name: Wells Fargo
scenes.headline: Incentives shape behaviour as powerfully as rules.
scenes.voiceover: The lesson: incentives can shape behaviour just as powerfully as rules.

scenes.headline: Theranos
scenes.voiceover: Number seven. Theranos. Twenty fifteen to twenty eighteen.

scenes.name: Theranos
scenes.headline: A blood test that didn't work as claimed
scenes.voiceover: Elizabeth Holmes claimed Theranos could perform hundreds of blood tests using tiny amounts of blood. Investors believed her, and the company reached a valuation of roughly nine billion dollars.

scenes.name: Theranos
scenes.headline: A famous board without the science to challenge her
scenes.voiceover: But employees and scientists raised concerns about the technology. The board contained many high-profile people, but lacked the scientific expertise needed to challenge the core claims effectively.

scenes.name: Theranos
scenes.headline: A journalist, backed by whistleblowers
scenes.voiceover: Journalist John Carreyrou investigated. His Wall Street Journal reporting, supported by whistleblower information, became a major turning point. Regulators followed, and the company collapsed.
scenes.body: Employees spoke, journalists investigated, regulators followed.

scenes.name: Theranos
scenes.headline: Prison, and $452 million in restitution
scenes.voiceover: Holmes was convicted and sentenced to one hundred and thirty-five months in prison. Former C O O Ramesh Balwani was convicted separately and sentenced to one hundred and fifty-five months. They were also ordered to pay approximately four hundred and fifty-two million dollars in restitution. Today, Theranos is gone, and both are serving prison sentences.

scenes.name: Theranos
scenes.headline: Famous names don't make a competent board.
scenes.voiceover: The lesson: a board full of famous names isn't necessarily a competent board.

scenes.headline: Wirecard
scenes.voiceover: Number eight. Wirecard. Twenty twenty.

scenes.name: Wirecard
scenes.headline: Auditors asked: where is the money?
scenes.voiceover: Wirecard looked like one of Europe's biggest fintech success stories. Then auditors asked a simple question: where is the money? Wirecard claimed around one point nine billion euros existed in trustee accounts. Auditors couldn't verify it.

scenes.name: Wirecard
scenes.headline: The money probably never existed
scenes.voiceover: Eventually, Wirecard admitted the money probably never existed, and the company collapsed. It was caught through investigative reporting, whistleblower allegations, and auditors being unable to verify the cash.

scenes.name: Wirecard
scenes.headline: The CEO charged. A top executive vanished.
scenes.voiceover: C E O Markus Braun was arrested and charged. Former executive Jan Marsalek disappeared, and became one of the world's most famous financial fugitives. The criminal trial against Braun and other former executives is still reaching its closing stage, so it isn't treated as a completed conviction.
scenes.body: Jan Marsalek remains wanted. Braun's trial has not reached a final verdict.

scenes.name: Wirecard
scenes.headline: Show me the money.
scenes.voiceover: The lesson: sometimes governance comes down to one simple question. Show me the money.

scenes.headline: Boeing 737 MAX
scenes.voiceover: Number nine. The Boeing seven-three-seven MAX. Twenty eighteen to twenty nineteen.

scenes.name: Boeing
scenes.headline: A new system pilots weren't properly told about
scenes.voiceover: The Boeing seven-three-seven MAX was developed under enormous commercial pressure. A new flight-control system called M CAS was introduced, but critical information about its behaviour and training requirements was not adequately communicated.

scenes.name: Boeing
scenes.headline: Two crashes in five months
scenes.voiceover: Lion Air Flight six-ten crashed in October twenty eighteen, killing one hundred and eighty-nine people. Five months later, Ethiopian Airlines Flight three-oh-two crashed, killing one hundred and fifty-seven. Three hundred and forty-six people died.

scenes.name: Boeing
scenes.headline: Grounded worldwide. Criminal proceedings followed.
scenes.voiceover: Investigations exposed failures involving aircraft design, pilot information, training, certification and safety oversight. The MAX was grounded worldwide. Boeing faced enormous legal and financial consequences, while the U S Department of Justice pursued criminal proceedings concerning the certification process. Litigation surrounding the crashes continued into twenty twenty-six.

scenes.name: Boeing
scenes.headline: Back in service, still rebuilding trust
scenes.voiceover: The MAX returned to service after changes and regulatory scrutiny. Boeing survived, but has been rebuilding its safety culture and its relationship with regulators.

scenes.name: Boeing
scenes.headline: When safety competes with commercial pressure, safety has to win.
scenes.voiceover: The lesson: when safety competes with commercial pressure, safety has to win.

scenes.headline: Punjab National Bank
scenes.voiceover: And number ten. Punjab National Bank. Twenty eleven to twenty eighteen.

scenes.name: Punjab National Bank
scenes.headline: Two systems that didn't talk to each other
scenes.voiceover: Punjab National Bank had a dangerous technology and control gap. Its SWIFT messaging system was not properly integrated with its core banking system. Fraudsters exploited that weakness to issue fraudulent Letters of Undertaking.
scenes.body: SWIFT messages never matched against core banking records.

scenes.name: Punjab National Bank
scenes.headline: A fraud that grew for years
scenes.voiceover: The alleged scheme grew for years and involved diamond businessmen Nirav Modi and Mehul Choksi. The fraud was eventually estimated at roughly thirteen thousand crore rupees.

scenes.name: Punjab National Bank
scenes.headline: Guarantees issued without collateral
scenes.voiceover: P N B discovered suspicious guarantees being issued without the required collateral, and investigators then uncovered the larger scheme. But by the time the scandal became public in twenty eighteen, key individuals had already left India.

scenes.name: Punjab National Bank
scenes.headline: Arrests abroad. Extradition fights continue.
scenes.voiceover: Nirav Modi was arrested in Britain in twenty nineteen, and continued fighting extradition. Mehul Choksi was arrested in Belgium in twenty twenty-five, after India's extradition request. International legal proceedings and asset recovery continue.

scenes.name: Punjab National Bank
scenes.headline: Controls are only as strong as their connections.
scenes.voiceover: The lesson: a control system is only as strong as the connections between its components.

scenes.headline: Different industries. Same failure.
scenes.voiceover: So what do Enron, WorldCom, Lehman Brothers, F T X, Volkswagen, Wells Fargo, Theranos, Wirecard, Boeing and Punjab National Bank actually have in common? They are completely different industries, countries, technologies and people. But the pattern is remarkably similar.

scenes.headline: A warning ignored. A control that didn't work.
scenes.body: A board that didn't ask. An auditor too comfortable. An employee afraid to speak.
scenes.voiceover: The disaster usually didn't begin on the day the company collapsed. It began years earlier. A warning was ignored. A control wasn't working. A board didn't ask the right question. An auditor became too comfortable. An employee was afraid to speak. A regulator didn't connect the dots. Or management created incentives that encouraged people to do the wrong thing.

scenes.headline: Good governance catches problems before they become scandals.
scenes.voiceover: The deeper lesson is this: good governance is designed to detect problems before they become scandals. Internal controls aren't there to make reports look professional. Auditors aren't there simply to sign documents. Boards aren't there just to attend meetings. Compliance isn't there simply to slow a company down.

scenes.eyebrow: Someone must be able to say
scenes.headline: “Wait. That number doesn't make sense.”
scenes.body: Where did this money come from? Why are we doing this? What happens if this goes wrong?
scenes.voiceover: Someone must be able to say: Wait. That number doesn't make sense. Where did this money come from? Why are we doing this? What happens if this goes wrong?

scenes.headline: Not preventing every mistake. Stopping one from becoming a catastrophe.
scenes.voiceover: Every company on this list had opportunities to stop the disaster earlier. The real tragedy isn't that the warning signs existed. It's that they weren't strong enough, or weren't taken seriously enough, to stop what came next. That is the real meaning of corporate governance. Not preventing every mistake, but making sure that one mistake doesn't become a catastrophe.

endcard.title: They knew.
